info.title: MarketBox 2.0 Open API
info.description: The MarketBox public API for building booking experiences. Core model: create an order, then draw its order items down into bookings. Single bookings reference an order item per service line; package bookings draw one PACKAGE item down across N sessions. To schedule a package, build a slate (POST /availability/package-slate) and book it by slateId (POST /orders/{orderId}/package-bookings). See the guides for end-to-end walkthroughs.

ApiKeyAuth.name: x-api-key
ApiKeyAuth.description: API key minted in the MarketBox dashboard. Scope is restricted to the projects you select at creation time.

feeId.description: Stable identifier for this fee, unique within the business model.

name.description: Buyer-facing label, rendered as its own line on the order summary.

calculation.description: How a service fee is calculated. FLAT charges a fixed amount; PERCENT charges a percentage of the pre-tax total of the lines the fee governs.

amount.description: FLAT fees only. Integer minor units, charged in whatever currency the order is placed in — 2500 is CA$25.00 on a CAD order and US$25.00 on a USD one. Use a PERCENT fee if you need it to scale.

percentage.description: PERCENT fees only. Applied to the pre-tax total of this business model's lines on the order.

taxable.description: When true, the fee is taxed at the rate the governing lines already resolved for their region. A taxable fee on a PACKAGE-only order resolves to zero tax: package lines are tax-exempt, so there is no rate to inherit.

priceRuleId.description: Which regional price rule this line resolved to. Compare against the offering/package `pricing[]` to see exactly which price was applied.

priceScope.description: Specificity of the matched rule: DEFAULT, COUNTRY, STATE or POSTAL. DEFAULT means no regional rule matched and the fallback price was used.

scope.description: How specifically a price rule targets a region. Resolution picks the most specific match: POSTAL beats STATE beats COUNTRY beats DEFAULT. DEFAULT is the fallback every offering must define ("any region"). On an order item, `priceScope` reports which one actually applied — seeing DEFAULT where you expected a regional price means the region did not resolve.

discountPercent.description: Percentage discount (0-100) recorded when this package's prices were seeded from the offering's prices (price = offering price * creditCount * (1 - discountPercent/100)). Informational metadata only: `pricing` is the authoritative source of the amounts charged. Individual prices can be manually overridden after seeding, and the offering's prices may change later, so this value is not guaranteed to match the actual prices - never derive amounts from it.

status.description: Lifecycle of the package bundle. ARCHIVED hides it from the storefront and blocks new orders, but order items already placed against it stay bookable.

post.summary: Create a new booking
post.description: Creates a single booking. Each service line must reference an existing order + order item (orderId + orderItemId) to draw down — create and pay for an order first. Location fields depend on locationType: TRAVEL_ZONE requires locationId, latitude, longitude, and a structured address; PHYSICAL requires only locationId; VIRTUAL requires none. Local-time fields are derived server-side from bookingTz and must not be sent.

patch.description: Moves a booking in time, or edits its details. Send UTC times (`bookingStartUtc`, `bookingEndUtc`) with `bookingTz`; the four local-time fields are computed from those and are deliberately NOT accepted here — passing local times directly is how a booking ends up disagreeing with itself across timezones. Rescheduling re-checks supplier availability, so a slot taken in the meantime is rejected rather than double-booked. Returns 409 if the booking changed underneath you.

post.summary: Change a booking status
post.description:
Moves the booking through its lifecycle. Only these transitions are allowed, and anything else is a 400:

- `SCHEDULED` -> `STARTED`, `CANCELLED`, `NO_SHOW`
- `STARTED` -> `COMPLETED`, `CANCELLED`
- `COMPLETED`, `CANCELLED`, `NO_SHOW` -> nothing

The last three are terminal: a completed, cancelled or no-showed booking cannot be reopened, so create a new booking instead. Cancelling releases the supplier time; for a package session it also returns the credit to the order item. Returns 409 if the booking changed underneath you.

post.summary: Create a new order
post.description: Creates an order (a cart/purchase record). For a package, add an item with { skuType: "PACKAGE", packageId } — the server derives service, offering, session count (creditCount), price and expiry from the package. For a single session use { skuType: "SINGLE_SESSION", serviceId, offeringId, quantity }. The order item is the credit ledger: its quantityRemaining is what bookings draw down. Currency is fixed at creation.

currency.description: ISO 4217 currency you quoted the buyer. Verified against the price the server resolves for this order's region; a mismatch is a 400.

reservationId.description: The hold this order funds. Preferred: the hold already knows where the booking happens, so the order and its bookings cannot disagree on price.

locationId.description: Stored Location for a PHYSICAL booking. Ignored when reservationId is given.

address.description: Service address for a TRAVEL_ZONE (in-home) booking. Ignored when reservationId or locationId is given.

skuType.description: What kind of line this is: SINGLE_SESSION, PACKAGE, SUBSCRIPTION, MEMBERSHIP, or DEPOSIT.

packageId.description: Required for PACKAGE items. serviceId, offeringId, session count, price and expiry are all derived from the package.

priceRuleId.description: Which regional price rule this line resolved to. Compare against the offering/package `pricing[]` to see exactly which price was applied.

priceScope.description: Specificity of the matched rule: DEFAULT, COUNTRY, STATE or POSTAL. DEFAULT means no regional rule matched and the fallback price was used.

feeId.description: The fee as configured on the business model.

businessModelId.description: The business model that levied this fee — the commercial definition the charge belongs to.

name.description: Buyer-facing label, snapshotted at purchase time.

calculation.description: How a service fee is calculated. FLAT charges a fixed amount; PERCENT charges a percentage of the pre-tax total of the lines the fee governs.

percentage.description: Echoed for PERCENT fees so the buyer can be shown the rate that applied (e.g. "Admin fee (5%)"). Absent for FLAT fees.

basis.description: Pre-tax total of this business model's lines — what a PERCENT fee was calculated against. Reported for FLAT fees too, so the figure is auditable.

tax.description: Tax on this fee, at the rate its governing lines resolved. Zero when the fee is not taxable, and zero on a package-only order because package lines are tax-exempt and carry no rate to inherit.

fees.description: Service fees levied by the business models on this order. Each is a discrete charge in its own right, NOT folded into `taxTotal` or `subtotal`. Applied once per fee however many lines it governs.

feeTotal.description: Sum of `fees[].amount`. Sits outside `subtotal`, so `total = subtotal + feeTotal + taxTotal`.

get.summary: List orders for a project by status
get.description: `status` is REQUIRED, not a convenience filter: orders are indexed by status, so there is no way to page every order in a project in one call. To list one client's orders instead, use `GET /projects/{projectId}/clients/{clientId}/orders`, which needs no status.

get.description:
The supplier directory, each row already carrying its resolved `services` and `skills`, so a "who can do X, near Y" page needs one call. Every filter is AND, both within a parameter and across parameters: `services=a,b` means a supplier offering BOTH, never either. post.summary: List a service's packages, each with a ready-to-book slate
post.description:
Returns every ACTIVE package of a service, each with a complete N-session plan built from a supplier's real availability. The response entry carries a slateId that can be booked directly via POST /orders/{orderId}/package-bookings. Cadence defaults to FREQ=WEEKLY;COUNT={creditCount}, derived per package. Packages that cannot be planned come back with status NO_COMPLETE_SLATE or NO_AVAILABILITY and a reason — they do not fail the request.

The rrule is the PREFERRED cadence, not a hard filter — set cadenceFlexibility to FALLBACK (or ALWAYS) and it applies to every package in the response. An entry that has no complete plan on the requested days then comes back with status ALTERNATIVE_CADENCE and a non-empty cadenceAlternatives: complete slates at a denser, supplier-feasible cadence, sorted closest-first by cadenceDistance. Read the outcome from each entry's status: NO_COMPLETE_SLATE is NO LONGER the only non-OK outcome, and ALTERNATIVE_CADENCE is a success — every cadenceAlternatives entry carries a slateId that is bookable in exactly the same way as primarySlate. A caller who does not set cadenceFlexibility sees no change at all: it defaults to NONE and cadenceAlternatives comes back empty.

post.summary: Reschedule a suggested slot to a new time (server-validated), refreshing its slate
post.description:
Moves ONE slot of a proposed slate to a time the client picked, before anything is booked. This is the "actually, can we do Thursday instead" step of a multi-session proposal — it does not touch bookings, which have their own reschedule route. The new time is validated against the supplier's real availability rather than trusted, and on success the parent slate's aggregates are recomputed and the whole updated slate is returned, so re-render from this response instead of patching the one slot locally.

Nearly everything that goes wrong is a 409, and the four causes need different handling — branch on the `code`, never on the status alone. The time may be held or booked on the supplier's calendar, in which case the body names the blocking reservation or booking. The supplier may simply not work then, though the time is valid and in the future. You may have lost a race to a concurrent hold, which returns SLOT_NO_LONGER_FREE and is worth one retry at a different time. Or the suggestion itself may have expired — and that response carries a freshly computed set of suggestions with it, so re-render those rather than starting a new availability search. A past or malformed `bookingStartUtc` is a 400.

post.summary: Hold supplier time during checkout — a single session, or a whole package slate
post.description: Claims supplier time so nobody else can book it while your client pays. Provide exactly one of: intervals (explicit supplier time — this is the form that works for a SINGLE session, with no package and no slate), slateId (hold every slot of a persisted package slate), or slotIds (cherry-pick slots of a slate). Every interval is claimed in ONE transaction, so a hold is all-or-nothing — you never end up holding 3 sessions of a 5-session package. Expiry is LAZY: nothing runs at heldUntil, the hold simply stops blocking, so convert before then. To HEARTBEAT a checkout page, re-post the same intervals AND the reservationId you were given (with the same heldBy): that EXTENDS the existing hold — heldUntil moves out, the same reservationId comes back, and no second hold is minted. Omitting reservationId always mints a NEW hold. Returns 409 with code SLOT_HELD/SLOT_BOOKED — naming the blocking reservationId or bookingId — when the time is already claimed, or RESERVATION_NOT_FOUND / RESERVATION_NOT_HELD / RESERVATION_FORBIDDEN when the reservationId you asked to extend is unknown, no longer held, or not yours.

post.summary: Convert a hold into confirmed bookings (the idempotent purchase hook)
post.description: Turns the held supplier time into real bookings, drawing credits from the given order item. The order item's skuType decides what is booked: a PACKAGE item books every held interval as package sessions; a SINGLE_SESSION item books the ONE held interval as an ordinary single booking — no package, and no 1-credit "reservation vehicle" package needed. (A SINGLE_SESSION item against a hold covering more than one interval returns 409 RESERVATION_MULTI_INTERVAL; any other skuType returns 400.) Call it from your payment webhook: it is idempotent on the reservationId (the package booking write uses the deterministic key convert:<reservationId>), so a webhook firing twice replays the same bookings rather than double-booking, and a reservation already CONVERTED replays its stored result. The bookings are rebuilt from the RESERVATION and the ORDER ITEM — never by re-resolving a suggestion that may have expired — so the booked service and the credit it draws down cannot disagree. Returns 409 HOLD_EXPIRED if you converted too late (the hold no longer blocks anyone), or SLOT_HELD/SLOT_BOOKED if someone else took the time in the meantime. This response is NOT wrapped in a { data } envelope, and created[].sessionIndex is 0-based.

post.summary: Add a service address to the caller's client profile
post.description:
Saves a service address for the signed-in client. Requires both the API key and the client user JWT, and the caller must already be onboarded — POST /clients/me first, or this is a 404.

The address id is derived from the address content, so this is an upsert, not an append: posting the same address twice returns the same id and leaves one record, while changing so much as a street number creates a second. The first address a client saves silently becomes their default; later ones do not displace it, so use the default route to move it rather than expecting the newest to win.

This matters beyond delivery: the default address is the last-resort source of the pricing region for an order that pins no reservation, location or explicit address. A client with no saved address resolves to no region at all and is priced at the offering's DEFAULT rule, in the DEFAULT rule's currency — which is how a client abroad ends up quoted in the wrong currency and rejected. Save the address before the first order.

post.summary: Add an offering to a service
post.description: The offering is the sellable variant — price and duration live here, not on the service, so this is the call that makes a service purchasable. It is created ACTIVE; there is no draft step. `pricing` is a rule hierarchy, not a single amount: exactly one DEFAULT rule is required, a STATE rule is rejected without a COUNTRY rule for the same country, and a POSTAL rule is rejected without the matching STATE rule. `country` and `state` accept full names and are stored as ISO codes ("Canada" becomes "CA", "Ontario" becomes "ON"), so read back what you wrote rather than assuming your spelling survived. Anything an order cannot match a region rule for falls through to DEFAULT — including its currency, which is why a catalogue sold abroad needs a COUNTRY rule per currency and not just a translated name. Every id in `skillIds` and `locationIds` must already exist and be active in the project, or the whole call is a 400.

post.summary: Record a manual (cash/external/comp) transaction against an order
post.description:
Books money that moved outside Stripe — cash at the door, a bank transfer, a comped session. Card payments do not belong here: `source` accepts only CASH, EXTERNAL and COMP, and STRIPE is rejected, because Stripe rows are created by the payment-intent flow and settled by webhook. `kind: "REFUND"` is likewise rejected; refunds are not yet supported.

The two kinds behave differently and the difference is easy to miss. PAYMENT adds to the order's `amountPaid` in the same atomic write, so it changes what the order still owes. ADJUSTMENT records a ledger row and leaves `amountPaid` alone — use it for corrections you want visible in history without moving the balance. Either way the row is written SUCCEEDED immediately, with no pending state to poll.

`amount.currency` must equal the order's currency exactly or the call is a 400; the order's currency is fixed at creation and cannot be converted here. A 409 means the order changed between this call reading it and writing — re-read the order and retry, rather than assuming the payment was recorded. `clientId` defaults to the order's client.

The filters are not combinable, and this is the mistake to avoid: exactly one of `orderId`, `clientId` and `status` takes effect, in that order of precedence, and the others are ignored without an error. Results are paginated with an opaque cursor that is only valid for the same filters that produced it. Both settled and unsettled rows come back, so sum only `status: "SUCCEEDED"` when computing what was actually collected — a PENDING Stripe row is an intent, not money.

post.summary: Create a Stripe PaymentIntent for an order (client-side confirmation)
post.description:
Starts a card payment for whatever the order still owes. Returns a `clientSecret` to confirm with Stripe.js in the browser — the card details never reach this API. The charge is created on the project's connected account for `total - amountPaid`, so part-paid orders are billed only for the remainder and a fully-paid order is a 400.

Safe to call more than once: if an open PENDING intent already exists for the order, its existing `clientSecret` is returned instead of a second intent being created, so a user who reloads checkout is not charged twice. Reuse means the amount comes from the original intent, though — if the order total changed in between, cancel the outstanding intent rather than expecting a fresh figure here.

The order must be DRAFT or PENDING; anything further along its lifecycle is a 400. A 409 means the project has no Stripe account connected or is not yet cleared to take charges, which is a setup problem no retry will fix. Confirming the intent does NOT settle the transaction here: the row stays PENDING until Stripe's webhook confirms it, so treat payment as complete only once the transaction reads SUCCEEDED.
